title: Buddha (as the tradition tells it)
tomorrow: Sam says 'so the Buddha was a Hindu god.' Dawa goes quiet. now what?

segments.voice: Yesterday, the Buddha in Jayadeva's verse: a heart with compassion, stopping at the creature on the altar. Today, one more verse, and a look back over the week.

Some messages are short enough for a sticky note and still start years of argument. The Bhagavata Purana gives the Buddha exactly that much room. In its first list of Vishnu's descents, one verse: at the start of the Kali age, he will be born as Buddha, the son of Anjana, among the Kikatas, to bewilder the enemies of the gods. That's all of it. When, whose son, where, and why.
screen: `A STICKY NOTE'S WORTH OF TEXT.` → `WHEN, WHOSE, WHERE, WHY.`

segments.voice: The why is the part readers have argued over. Some take it just as it stands: a teaching meant to lead astray those set against the gods. Yesterday's poet sang a very different Buddha, moved by compassion. So one name holds two Hindu faces, and Buddhists tell him a third way, as their own teacher. Now the week, in order. Rama on the beach, whose door stayed open even to his enemy's brother. Krishna born in a prison, hidden at his mother's plea, light enough to be carried. One small but: krishnas tu bhagavan svayam, read two ways by two schools, both with love. Yuge yuge: he comes age after age, whenever dharma slips. Don't be afraid, get up: the wounded one steadying the hunter. And a compassionate heart that stops at the frightened animal. Six turns. Each one walks into a different trouble wearing a different face, and the Bhagavata's single verse is a reminder that some of those faces come with very few words attached.
screen: `ONE VERSE: WHEN, WHOSE, WHERE, WHY.` · `TWO HINDU FACES, ONE NAME.` · `THE WEEK: SIX TURNS.` · `A DIFFERENT FACE FOR EACH TROUBLE.` · then, large: `AS THE TRADITION TELLS IT.`

segments.voice: Close your eyes and let the week's pictures pass once, slowly: a beach at night, a prison door, a small word, a conch, an arrow, an altar. Don't hold on to any of them. When they've gone by, rest in the quiet they leave for the rest of the sit.
Buddha: in the Bhagavata, one verse, born among the Kikatas at the start of the Kali age; in Jayadeva, a compassionate heart.
Hold onto this: Buddha, as the tradition tells it, one verse with four details and more than one face. A week ends here.

fork.reveal: Krishna tells Jara: don't be afraid, get up; this happened by my own wish. The wounded one steadies the other.

chat.says: Sam's grandma mailed Nani a card: 'I was a stranger, and ye took me in.' that's Rama's thing, right??
options: close: both honor taking in the one at the door, each in its own book and words.
it's the same teaching, so the Bible and the Ramayana are one story.

chat.meaning: Rama vowed to shelter whoever comes asking; the card quotes Jesus in Matthew 25. Both honor welcoming the one at the door, each in its own words.

Kikatas.meaning: the people among whom the Bhagavata places the Buddha's birth

Anjana.meaning: named in the Bhagavata as the Buddha's parent

Kali age.meaning: the dark age that began when Krishna left

Bhagavata Purana.meaning: a Purana of Vishnu's descents and Krishna's life
